newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks rise on news of Kessler exit.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks rise on news of Kessler exit.

text.p: Tobacco shares ended broadly higher in Monday trading, as investors celebrated the news that David Kessler, chief of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and a vocal anti-smoking advocate, intends to leave his post.

Philip Morris Cos Inc, the maker of Marlboro cigarettes, jumped 3-1/8 to 105-1/2; RJR Nabisco Holdings, which makes Camels, gained 5/8 to 32; Loews Corp, which owns Lorillard, was up 3-5/8 to 94-5/8; and UST Inc added 7/8 to 32-3/4.
Kessler will leave his post in early 1997 after a successor has been named, according to FDA officials.
Tobacco industry analysts said Kessler's departure would have little effect on the industry. Emanuel Goldman at PaineWebber characterized the development as "the removal of a negative situation."
Whether tobacco companies are helped or hurt by his exit "depends on who takes over. Certainly his leaving is not going to hurt tobacco companies," Goldman said.
Goldman said a Republican-controlled Congress or the courts could still block FDA efforts to regulate the industry.

Roy Burry, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, said that since the Clinton administration is behind the FDA's efforts, the departure by Kessler will have little effect, because his successor will take the same stance.
"Any head of the FDA is going to be totally anti-tobacco and health oriented," Burry said. "I don't think Kessler's leaving is going to have any effect."
Burry noted that a U.S. federal court in February will consider whether the FDA has jurisdiction to regulate the tobacco industry.
Analysts said that a more important arena is the tobacco litigation that is pending in courts around the U.S.

Some money managers lauded the development. Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood, saw it as "a major plus...for tobacco stocks. This vendetta they've had against the tobacco companies will probably lose some of its steam."
Led by Kessler, who has been strongly critical of tobacco companies, the FDA has been considering a plan to regulate tobacco as a drug delivery device.
Kessler has asserted that the tobacco industry knew of and exploited the fact that smokers are addicted to nicotine.

Proposed U.S. rules on tobacco seek to keep children from starting smoking by limiting their access to tobacco, reducing the appeal of advertising to youngsters, and limiting the sale of child-oriented products, such as caps or bags with tobacco company logos.
